neutral_facts.value: The accused, a daily wages worker, married a woman shortly before the incident. The couple resided in a rented house due to poverty. On the day of the incident, the accused questioned the victim about her return time, suspecting her fidelity. The accused assaulted her with fists and kicks, then poured kerosene over her and set her on fire. The victim suffered severe burns and later succumbed to her injuries. The victim's dying declaration, along with the testimony of her family members and neighbors, established the accused's actions. A post-mortem report confirmed the cause of death as shock and septicaemia from the burns. The accused attempted to extinguish the fire by pouring water on the victim, but this act was not considered a mitigating factor as it was seen as an attempt to conceal his guilt.

prosecution_argument.value: The prosecution argued that the accused, suspecting his wife of infidelity, assaulted her and set her on fire by pouring kerosene over her, leading to her death. The evidence, including the dying declaration and oral testimony of witnesses, established the guilt of the accused beyond reasonable doubt.

quotes.text: The accused suspected the deceased of infidelity and picking up a fight over it, he kicked her and inflicted fist blows and further set her on fire by pouring kerosene over her person.

defence_argument.value: The defence contended that the fire was accidental, and the accused tried to extinguish it, indicating no intention to kill. They also relied on the case of Kalu Ram vs. State of Rajasthan to argue that the act of pouring water would mitigate the offence.

quotes.text: It was submitted that in any event, there was no pre-meditation and there was no intention on the part of the appellant to kill his wife and the facts and circumstances show that the appellant could not have intended to cause the death of deceased.

legal_principle_applied.value: The court applied the principle that an act amounting to murder is one where the intention to kill is present. If such intention is absent, the act may be culpable homicide not amounting to murder. However, the court emphasized that the act of causing injury so imminently dangerous that it will in all probability cause death constitutes murder.

quotes.text: Where the intention to kill is present, the act amounts to murder, where such an intention is absent, the act amounts to culpable homicide not amounting to murder.

sentencing_rationale.value: The court imposed the maximum penalty prescribed by law to serve as a deterrent against such crimes, especially in bride burning cases, where the guilt of the accused is established beyond reasonable doubt.

quotes.text: In bride burning cases, whenever the guilt of the accused is brought home beyond reasonable doubt, it is the duty of the Court to deal with it sternly and award the maximum penalty prescribed by the law in order that it may operate as a deterrent to other persons from committing such offence.

judicial_aggravating_factors.value: The court considered the aggravating factor of the crime being a bride burning case, where the deceased died within three months of her marriage, highlighting the societal and moral gravity of the act.

quotes.text: Within three months of her marriage, the deceased died of burn injuries. In bride burning cases, whenever the guilt of the accused is brought home beyond reasonable doubt, it is the duty of the Court to deal with it sternly and award the maximum penalty prescribed by the law in order that it may operate as a deterrent to other persons from committing such offence.
